summary: Specifies BGPsec, an extension to BGP that secures the AS path in UPDATE messages. Each AS that passes on the message adds a digital signature in an optional non-transitive path attribute, which shows that every AS on the path authorized the advertisement.

plainLanguage.summary: BGPsec adds signatures to BGP route advertisements so a receiver can check that each AS on the listed path chose to pass the route onward. It relies on RPKI router certificates and protects the route advertisement, not the path that later data packets take.

how does bgpsec sign an as path
subtitle: Digital signatures let BGP speakers check which autonomous systems propagated a route.

tldr.problem: A BGP route advertisement lists the AS path but does not show whether each AS on that path authorized passing the route to the next AS.
tldr.mechanism: BGPsec replaces AS_PATH with an optional BGPsec_PATH attribute containing a Secure_Path and signatures. Each AS signs the route for its next AS, and receivers check signatures using RPKI router certificates.
tldr.outcome: A valid message provides assurance about the path taken by the UPDATE, not the path taken by data packets. RFC 8205 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8206.

today: RFC 8205 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8206. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What BGPsec Adds to BGP
sections.content:
BGPsec provides path security for BGP route advertisements. A receiver of a valid BGPsec UPDATE can verify that each AS on the listed path authorized advertising the route to the next AS.

The route path and its signatures are carried in the optional, non-transitive BGPsec_PATH attribute. BGPsec is intended to supplement BGP origin validation; together the mechanisms can prevent many route-hijacking attacks.

A speaker sending BGPsec UPDATEs to external peers needs a private key associated with an RPKI router certificate for its AS number. A speaker can validate received BGPsec messages without holding such a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: BGPsec lets a receiving router check that each network on a route agreed to pass the advertisement onward. The signatures use keys linked to AS numbers by RPKI router certificates.

sections.title: Negotiating BGPsec Support
sections.content:
BGP speakers advertise BGPsec support in an OPEN message using capability code 7, with a capability length of 3 octets. The capability identifies the BGPsec version, whether the speaker can send or receive BGPsec UPDATEs, and an address family.

The direction bit is 1 for sending and 0 for receiving. Two capabilities are needed for both directions. RFC 8205 defines version 0 and the IPv4 and IPv6 address families, with AFI values 1 and 2.

A speaker may send BGPsec UPDATEs only when the sender advertised send capability and the receiver advertised receive capability for the same version and address family. Both peers must also support the multiprotocol extension for that family and four-octet AS numbers. Traditional unsigned UPDATEs remain permitted if BGPsec was not negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: Before exchanging signed routes, each router advertises whether it can send or receive them. A sender may use BGPsec only when the other router advertised that it can receive it.

sections.title: The BGPsec_PATH Attribute
sections.content:
BGPsec_PATH replaces AS_PATH; an UPDATE must contain one or the other, not both. The attribute contains a Secure_Path followed by one or two Signature_Blocks. Two blocks support a transition between algorithm suites.

The Secure_Path has a length followed by one six-octet segment per distinct AS. Each segment contains an eight-bit pCount, a flags octet and a four-octet AS number. pCount represents repetitions of an AS, allowing path prepending without repeating signatures.

Each Signature_Block identifies an algorithm suite and contains one Signature Segment for every Secure_Path segment. A Signature Segment contains a 20-octet Subject Key Identifier (SKI), a two-octet signature length and the signature bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute stores the AS path and a matching signature for each AS. A segment can also record that an AS was repeated without requiring that AS to create repeated signatures.

sections.title: Building and Signing a Route
sections.content:
A BGPsec UPDATE advertises one prefix and encodes it with MP_REACH_NLRI. Since a signature includes the AS number of the receiving peer, a speaker sends a separate BGPsec UPDATE to each distinct peer AS.

When forwarding to an external peer, the speaker adds a Secure_Path segment for its AS and a signature segment. The signature covers the target AS, earlier path and signature segments, algorithm suite, address family, subfamily and prefix. The speaker needs a private key whose certificate names its AS.

A route server that does not carry traffic as a transit AS may set pCount to 0 while still including and signing its AS number. If a route must be sent to a peer without BGPsec support, the sender reconstructs AS_PATH and sends an unsigned UPDATE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each AS adds its number and signs the route for the specific AS that will receive it. A router sends a different signed update to each destination AS.

sections.title: Checking Received Signatures
sections.content:
A BGPsec speaker should validate UPDATEs received from external peers. It first checks that the attribute is well formed, that the most recent AS matches the sending peer, that there is a signature segment for each path segment, and that AS_PATH is absent. It also checks confederation flags, pCount rules and AS-loop conditions.

For each supported algorithm suite, the speaker checks signatures from the most recent AS toward the origin. It finds the matching AS number, public key and SKI in valid RPKI router certificate data, reconstructs the signed bytes and verifies the signature. A failed signature makes that block Not Valid; one valid block is enough for the UPDATE to be Valid.

Malformed path attributes are handled as treat-as-withdraw. The validity result depends on current RPKI data, so affected stored routes must be revalidated when that data changes. Local policy decides how the result affects route selection.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the route structure, then verifies the signatures against RPKI router certificates. If any supported signature block verifies, the UPDATE is valid; operators decide how that result affects route choice.

sections.title: Algorithms and Partial Deployment
sections.content:
Peers do not negotiate an algorithm suite just for their session, because every later speaker receiving the route must understand it. RFC 8208 specifies a current suite. During a suite transition, speakers can carry signatures for both suites, and a speaker must retain an invalid block when forwarding a route that has another valid block.

Operators need to configure when pCount may be zero, because an unexpected zero can be an error and misuse could make a route appear shorter. A fresh high-entropy secret random number is required for every ECDSA signature with P-256. The RFC also describes local RPKI data for private AS numbers.

During partial deployment, a speaker that cannot send BGPsec to the next AS converts the route to an unsigned UPDATE. The path assurance therefore ends at that point; contiguous groups of BGPsec speakers can still protect routes within their group.
sections.plainLanguage: All routers that receive a signed route need to understand its algorithm, so algorithm changes require coordination. If the route reaches a router that does not support BGPsec, the signatures are removed and later routers no longer have that path proof.

sections.title: Security Guarantees and Limits
sections.content:
Used with origin validation, a valid BGPsec UPDATE shows that the origin AS was authorized for the prefix and that each AS on the path intentionally propagated the route to the next AS. It proves the route advertisement followed the listed AS path; it does not prove that data packets use that path.

The signatures do not say that an AS validated earlier signatures. RPKI views may differ, so one router can judge an UPDATE Not Valid while another judges it Valid. Colluding ASes can tunnel messages, and BGPsec does not protect the BGP transport connection.

Signature checks can consume resources, so the RFC recommends doing cheaper validation first and stopping signature verification after an invalid signature. It also recommends transport security for BGP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid update proves that the listed ASes authorized the route advertisement, not that traffic will follow the same route. BGPsec also does not prevent colluding networks from tunneling updates or protect the connection carrying them.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Only version 0 is defined in this RFC.

fields.name: Unassigned
fields.desc: Sender sets these bits to zero.

fields.name: pCount
fields.desc: Number of AS repetitions covered by this signature.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Top bit is Confed_Segment; the other bits are unassigned and zero.

fields.name: AS Number
fields.desc: AS that added this path segment.
